particular spot excites or inhibits the neuron, then that location is part of the neuron’s excitatory or inhibitory receptive field.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":36},{"text":"In the simplest case, a ganglion cell’s receptive field has a circular center and an antagonistic doughnutshaped surround.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":37},{"text":"The magnocellular neurons, with larger receptive fields, respond to movement and overall patterns, but not color or fine details.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":38},{"text":"Other visual cells derive their receptive fields from the connections they receive.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":131},{"text":"For analogy, suppose you keep track of events on a city block.","printedPage":163,"pdfPage":181,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":132},{"text":"Bipolar cells report to a ganglion cell, which therefore has a larger receptive field, as illustrated in Figure 5.17.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":133},{"text":"The receptive field might be excited by light in the center and inhibited by light in the surround, or the opposite.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":134},{"text":"Some ganglion cells respond only to a stimulus moving in a particular direction.","printedPage":164,"pdfPage":182,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":135},{"text":"(Parvocellular means “small celled,” from the Latin root parv, meaning “small.”) Magnocellular neurons, with larger cell bodies and receptive fields, are distributed evenly throughout the retina.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":136},{"text":"(Magnocellular means “large celled,” from the Latin root magn, meaning “large,” as in the word magnify.) The koniocellular neurons have small cell bodies, like the parvocellular neurons, but they occur throughout the retina.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":137}],"originalFacts":10,"additionalFacts":7,"glossary":[{"term":"Koniocellular neurons","definition":"small ganglion cells that occur throughout the retina","sourcePrintedPage":625,"sourcePdfPage":643},{"term":"Magnocellular neurons","definition":"large cell bodies with large receptive fields that are distributed evenly throughout the retina","sourcePrintedPage":626,"sourcePdfPage":644},{"term":"Parvocellular neurons","definition":"small cell bodies with small receptive fields in or near the fovea","sourcePrintedPage":629,"sourcePdfPage":647},{"term":"Receptive fields","definition":"the area in visual space that excites or inhibits any to the primary visual cortex in the occipital cortex, also known","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":40},{"text":"as area V1 or the striate cortex because of its striped appearance.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":41},{"text":"Activity from V1 projects to the frontal cortex, which within 100–200 milliseconds sends information back to modify the activity in V1 and other visual areas.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":42},{"text":"People with damage in and around area V1 report no conscious vision, no visual imagery, and no visual dreams .","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":43},{"text":"About 1 to 3 percent of people have no visual imagery at all, other than maybe in a dream now and then.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":44},{"text":"People with this condition, called aphantasia , tend to be attracted toward math and science.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":45},{"text":"Some people with damage to area V1 display a surprising phenomenon called blindsight , the ability to respond to visual information without perceiving it consciously.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":46},{"text":"Many patients respond in one of these ways and not the others, because of differences in which connections were damaged.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":47},{"text":"In one study, every patient with blindsight had intact connections from the visual area of the thalamus to the temporal cortex .","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":48},{"text":"Hyperphantasia is more common among women than men, and it tends to be associated with artistic and other creative occupations.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":138},{"text":"When you imagine a visual scene, the activity starts in the memory and language areas of the cortex, and then spreads gradually to V1.","printedPage":165,"pdfPage":183,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":139},{"text":"In any case, the conclusion remains that V1 and surrounding areas are essential for conscious vision.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":140},{"text":"Even if your brain is intact, you could experience something like blindsight under certain circumstances.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":141}],"originalFacts":9,"additionalFacts":4,"glossary":[{"term":"Lateral geniculate nucleus","definition":"thalamic nucleus that receives incoming visual information","sourcePrintedPage":626,"sourcePdfPage":644},{"term":"Ganglion cells","definition":"type of neuron in the retina that receives input from the bipolar cells","sourcePrintedPage":624,"sourcePdfPage":642},{"term":"Blindsight","definition":"the ability to respond in limited ways to visual information without and Complex Receptive Fields","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m5-2-h04","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"facts":[{"text":"In the 1950s, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel inserted thin electrodes to record activity from cells in cats’ and monkeys’ occipital cortex while they presented visual patterns to the retina.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":50},{"text":"The cell had a bar-shaped receptive field, rather than a circular receptive field like cells in the retina and lateral geniculate .","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":51},{"text":"Light in the excitatory zone increases responses and light in the inhibitory zone decreases it.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":52},{"text":"Most simple cells have bar-shaped or edge-shaped receptive fields in horizontal or vertical orientations.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":53},{"text":"Most complex cells respond mostly to a stimulus moving in a particular direction—for example, a vertical bar moving left to right.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":54},{"text":"The best way to classify a cell as simple or complex is to present a stimulus in several locations.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":55},{"text":"A cell that responds to a stimulus in only one location is a simple cell.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":56},{"text":"Later researchers found that a cortical cell that responds well to a single bar or line","printedPage":167,"pdfPage":185,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":57},{"text":"Many cortical neurons respond best to a particular spatial frequency of lines and hardly at all to other frequencies .","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":58},{"text":"How the brain codes vision does not match what we see in any very simple way.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":59},{"text":"The illustration shows the receptive field of a simple cell.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":142},{"text":"A simple cell has a receptive field with fixed excitatory and inhibitory zones.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":143},{"text":"Complex cells, located in areas V1 and V2, also respond to bars and edges, but they respond equally anywhere within a large receptive field.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":144},{"text":"An end-stopped or hypercomplex cell resembles a complex cell except that it has a strong inhibitory area at one end of its bar-shaped receptive field.","printedPage":166,"pdfPage":184,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":145},{"text":"From a mathematical standpoint, sine wave frequencies are easy to work with.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":146},{"text":"A branch of mathematics called Fourier analysis demonstrates that a combination of sine waves can produce an unlimited variety of other patterns.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":147},{"text":"Thus, a series of spatial frequency detectors, some sensitive to horizontal patterns and others to vertical patterns, could represent any possible display.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":148},{"text":"Still, we perceive the world as objects, not sine waves.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":149}],"originalFacts":10,"additionalFacts":8,"glossary":[{"term":"Receptive fields","definition":"the area in visual space that excites or inhibits any neuron","sourcePrintedPage":631,"sourcePdfPage":649},{"term":"Complex cell","definition":"type of visual cortex cell located in areas V1 and V2 that responds to a pattern of light in a particular orientation anywhere within its large receptive field","sourcePrintedPage":621,"sourcePdfPage":639},{"term":"Simple cell","definition":"type of visual cortex cell that has a receptive field with fixed excitatory and inhibitory zones","sourcePrintedPage":632,"sourcePdfPage":650},{"term":"Frequency","definition":"the Hz","sourcePrintedPage":623,"sourcePdfPage":641}],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":510,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":326},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-h06","title":"Are Visual Cortex Cells Feature Detectors?","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m5-2-h04","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"facts":[{"text":"Given that neurons in area V1 respond strongly to particular patterns, we might suppose that the activity of such a cell represents the perception of that pattern, such as lines or bars.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":61},{"text":"If so, such cells would be feature detectors —neurons whose responses indicate the presence of a particular feature.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":62},{"text":"Supporting the idea of feature detectors is the fact that prolonged exposure to a given visual feature decreases sensitivity to that feature, as if it fatigued the relevant detectors.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":63},{"text":"Long ago, Gestalt psychologists rejected the idea that feature detectors tell the whole story about our perceptions.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":64},{"text":"It is a top-down process in which other brain areas interpret the visual stimulus and send messages back to reorganize V1 activity.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":65},{"text":"In a sense, the brain is constantly forming hypotheses or expectations about the world, and then modifying them based on “prediction errors” when it compares the expectations to sensory input .","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":66},{"text":"For example, if you stare at a waterfall for a minute or more and then look away, the rocks and trees next to the waterfall appear to flow upward.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":150},{"text":"For example, if you examine Figure 5.22, you might at first see nothing.","printedPage":168,"pdfPage":186,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":151}],"originalFacts":6,"additionalFacts":2,"glossary":[],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":300,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":191},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-h07","title":"Development around.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":68},{"text":"Within months, however, you began to recognize faces and crawl toward your favorite toys.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":69},{"text":"In a newborn mammal, many properties of the visual system develop before birth .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":70},{"text":"Waves of spontaneous activity sweep over the developing retina, synchronizing the activity of neighboring receptors and enabling appropriate combinations of receptors to establish connections with cells in the brain .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":71},{"text":"A study of people who were born without eyes found that the connections from the primary visual cortex to its main targets were more or less normal .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":72},{"text":"Nevertheless, visual experience after birth is necessary for maintaining and modifying the connections.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":73},{"text":"Unless you were born blind, you did have this experience—on the day you were born!","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":152},{"text":"The young of mammals such as horses have to make sense of vision quickly, as they start walking and following their mother shortly after birth.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":153}],"originalFacts":6,"additionalFacts":2,"glossary":[],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":214,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":153},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-h08","title":"Deprived vision.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":75},{"text":"right because the exact distance between the eyes varies from experimenter sutures one eyelid shut for a kitten’s first 4 to 6 weeks of life, synapses in the visual cortex gradually become unresponsive to input from the deprived eye .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":77},{"text":"After an eye deprived of vision in adults is reopened, cells gradually return to their previous levels of responsiveness .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":78},{"text":"After the deprived eye is opened, the kitten does not respond to it.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":154},{"text":"A similar period of deprivation in older animals weakens the response to the deprived eye, but not as strongly as it does in young ones.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":155}],"originalFacts":4,"additionalFacts":2,"glossary":[],"sourceBodyWordsAvailable":186,"sourceStatus":"source_explained","mdCrosscheck":"terms_present","wordCount":144},{"id":"bp14-m5-2-h09","title":"Deprived not.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":80},{"text":"When just one eye is open, the synapses from the open eye release a chemical that inhibits the synapses from the closed eye .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":81},{"text":"For at least 3 weeks, the kitten’s cortex remains responsive to visual input, although most cells become responsive to just one eye or the other and not both .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":82},{"text":"If the eyes remain shut still longer, the cortical responses start to become sluggish and lose their well-defined receptive fields .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":83},{"text":"For each aspect of visual experience, researchers identify a sensitive period , when experiences have a particularly strong and enduring influence .","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":84},{"text":"infant into an older mouse could induce a new period of heightened susceptibility to experience .","printedPage":170,"pdfPage":188,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":85},{"text":"However, even long after the sensitive period, a prolonged experience—such as a full week without visual stimulation to one eye—produces a smaller but measurable effect on the visual cortex .","printedPage":170,"pdfPage":188,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":86},{"text":"If neither eye is active, no axon outcompetes any other.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":156},{"text":"Eventually, the visual cortex may start responding to auditory or touch stimuli instead.","printedPage":169,"pdfPage":187,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":157},{"text":"Cortical plasticity is greatest in early life, but it never ends.","printedPage":170,"pdfPage":188,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":158}],"originalFacts":7,"additionalFacts":3,"glossary":[{"term":"Receptive The bipolar cells to the sides (laterally) get no excitation but some inhibition.","Bipolar cells 7, 8, and 9 are inhibited by input on both sides, but bipolar cells 6 and 10 are inhibited from only one side, and therefore 6 and 10 respond the most. Bipolar cells 5 and 11 receive no excitation, but the horizontal cell inhibits them.","These results illustrate lateral inhibition, reduced activity in a neuron because of activity in neighboring neurons.","Each cell in the visual system of the brain has a receptive field, an area in visual space from which light excites or inhibits the cell.","The receptive field of a rod or cone is the point in space from which light strikes the cell.","Everyone on the street reports to a supervisor, whose receptive field is the whole street, the combined area of input.","All the street supervisors report to the neighborhood manager, whose receptive field is the whole neighborhood. Rods and cones with tiny receptive fields connect to a bipolar cell, with a receptive field that combines those of all cells connected to it,","The receptive fields of ganglion cells converge at the next level, and so on.","To find a cell’s receptive field, an investigator records from the cell while shining light in various locations.","If light on a particular spot excites or inhibits the neuron, then that location is part of the neuron’s excitatory or inhibitory receptive field. In the simplest case, a ganglion cell’s receptive field has a circular center and an antagonistic doughnutshaped surround.","The magnocellular neurons, with larger receptive fields, respond to movement and overall patterns, but not color or fine details.","Information goes from the ganglion cells to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus and then to the primary visual cortex in the occipital cortex, also known","as area V1 or the striate cortex because of its striped appearance.","Activity from V1 projects to the frontal cortex, which within 100–200 milliseconds sends information back to modify the activity in V1 and other visual areas.","People with damage in and around area V1 report no conscious vision, no visual imagery, and no visual dreams. About 1 to 3 percent of people have no visual imagery at all, other than maybe in a dream now and then.","People with this condition, called aphantasia, tend to be attracted toward math and science.","Some people with damage to area V1 display a surprising phenomenon called blindsight, the ability to respond to visual information without perceiving it consciously. Many patients respond in one of these ways and not the others, because of differences in which connections were damaged.","In one study, every patient with blindsight had intact connections from the visual area of the thalamus to the temporal cortex.","In the 1950s, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel inserted thin electrodes to record activity from cells in cats’ and monkeys’ occipital cortex while they presented visual patterns to the retina.","The cell had a bar-shaped receptive field, rather than a circular receptive field like cells in the retina and lateral geniculate.","Light in the excitatory zone increases responses and light in the inhibitory zone decreases it.","Most simple cells have bar-shaped or edge-shaped receptive fields in horizontal or vertical orientations. Most complex cells respond mostly to a stimulus moving in a particular direction—for example, a vertical bar moving left to right.","The best way to classify a cell as simple or complex is to present a stimulus in several locations.","A cell that responds to a stimulus in only one location is a simple cell.","Later researchers found that a cortical cell that responds well to a single bar or line Many cortical neurons respond best to a particular spatial frequency of lines and hardly at all to other frequencies.","How the brain codes vision does not match what we see in any very simple way.","Given that neurons in area V1 respond strongly to particular patterns, we might suppose that the activity of such a cell represents the perception of that pattern, such as lines or bars.","If so, such cells would be feature detectors —neurons whose responses indicate the presence of a particular feature.","Supporting the idea of feature detectors is the fact that prolonged exposure to a given visual feature decreases sensitivity to that feature, as if it fatigued the relevant detectors.","Long ago, Gestalt psychologists rejected the idea that feature detectors tell the whole story about our perceptions. It is a top-down process in which other brain areas interpret the visual stimulus and send messages back to reorganize V1 activity.","In a sense, the brain is constantly forming hypotheses or expectations about the world, and then modifying them based on “prediction errors” when it compares the expectations to sensory input.","Then, for the first time, you came out into the light and looked around.","Within months, however, you began to recognize faces and crawl toward your favorite toys.","In a newborn mammal, many properties of the visual system develop before birth.","Waves of spontaneous activity sweep over the developing retina, synchronizing the activity of neighboring receptors and enabling appropriate combinations of receptors to establish connections with cells in the brain. A study of people who were born without eyes found that the connections from the primary visual cortex to its main targets were more or less normal.","Nevertheless, visual experience after birth is necessary for maintaining and modifying the connections.","When a kitten opens its eyes at about age 9 days, each neuron responds to areas in the two retinas that focus on approximately the same point in space—a process necessary for binocular vision.","right because the exact distance between the eyes varies from one kitten to another, and the distance changes over age. If an experimenter sutures one eyelid shut for a kitten’s first 4 to 6 weeks of life, synapses in the visual cortex gradually become unresponsive to input from the deprived eye.","After an eye deprived of vision in adults is reopened, cells gradually return to their previous levels of responsiveness.","You might guess that the kitten would become insensitive to both eyes, but it does not.","When just one eye is open, the synapses from the open eye release a chemical that inhibits the synapses from the closed eye.","For at least 3 weeks, the kitten’s cortex remains responsive to visual input, although most cells become responsive to just one eye or the other and not both. If the eyes remain shut still longer, the cortical responses start to become sluggish and lose their well-defined receptive fields.","For each aspect of visual experience, researchers identify a sensitive period, when experiences have a particularly strong and enduring influence.","infant into an older mouse could induce a new period of heightened susceptibility to experience. However, even long after the sensitive period, a prolonged experience—such as a full week without visual stimulation to one eye—produces a smaller but measurable effect on the visual cortex.","Stereoscopic depth perception requires the brain to detect retinal disparity, the discrepancy between what the left and right eyes see.","During early development, each neuron in the visual cortex receives many inputs from both eyes, but it uses inhibitory synapses to suppress unmatching inputs.","The result is to make the neuron responsive to corresponding areas of the left and right eyes—areas that see the same thing at the same time. However, when the task was to feel a block and point to which of two choices was the picture of that block, the children’s performance was only a little better than chance.","Seeing well enough to ride a bicycle took a year and a half.","Some aspects of vision, such as motion perception and depth perception, never reached normal levels. The ventral and dorsal streams contribute differently to recognizing what an object is and guiding responses to its location and movement."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The sections on shape, face recognition, and motion show how different processing systems support different visual abilities. Compare their functions and the problems that appear when particular pathways are disrupted."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m5-3-study-1","text":"Two interacting visual streams"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After early visual processing, two broad networks contribute to distinct but interacting demands. The ventral stream is especially important for identifying and recognizing objects, including their shapes and identities. The dorsal stream contributes to spatial information and the visual guidance of actions. The familiar 'what' versus 'where/how' distinction is a helpful beginning, not a rule that the pathways never cooperate. Everyday activities such as reaching for a familiar object require information from both."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m5-3-study-2","text":"Shapes and faces"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Inferior temporal regions participate in recognizing complex visual patterns and distinguishing objects despite changes in appearance. Faces are especially important social stimuli, and injury or altered processing in relevant networks can produce striking recognition difficulties. Recognizing someone is not just detecting eyes and a nose; the brain integrates the arrangement of features, memory, and context. A visual recognition deficit does not imply that the person's eyes are defective."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m5-3-study-3","text":"Movement information"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Movement perception depends on changes in the visual pattern over space and time. Regions including the middle temporal area have important roles in processing motion. A person may have intact basic sight yet experience profound difficulty perceiving movement if relevant networks are damaged. This contrasts with a problem of acuity or color vision. Different impairments therefore reveal that visual experience consists of several partly separable computations."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m5-3-study-4","text":"Putting the pathways together"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The same moving face can be represented in terms of identity, location, motion, and significance. These are not four separate photographs in the head: they are coordinated neural processes. When studying disorders of vision, ask which operation is compromised—detecting stimulation, discriminating a feature, locating an object, guiding action, or recognizing identity. That question often predicts the pattern of preserved and impaired abilities better than a broad label such as 'blindness'."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-3-h01","text":"The Ventral and Dorsal Streams"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The ventral stream through the temporal cortex is the “what” pathway, because of its importance for identifying and recognizing objects.","sourcePrintedPage":176,"sourcePdfPage":194,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The dorsal stream through the parietal cortex is the “where” or “how” pathway, because of its importance for visually guided movements.","sourcePrintedPage":176,"sourcePdfPage":194,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The distinction is based partly on animal studies, partly on MRI and fMRI studies , and partly on observations of patients with brain damage.","sourcePrintedPage":176,"sourcePdfPage":194,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A woman known as DF was exposed to carbon monoxide, causing damage mainly to the ventral stream—that is, the temporal cortex and its connections with the primary visual cortex .","sourcePrintedPage":176,"sourcePdfPage":194,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, when asked to pick up the object, she reached out correctly, adjusting her thumb and finger before touching the object .","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Another patient had such trouble recognizing objects by sight that she attached distinctive colored tapes to the important objects she needed to find in her house.","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, she had no trouble reaching out to pick up any of the objects, once she had found it .","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, his accuracy was normal when aiming his left arm or leg toward either side, or when aiming his right arm toward the left side .","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although the distinction between ventral and dorsal streams is useful, we should not overstate it.","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-3-h02","text":"Shape Perception"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In Module 5.2, we encountered simple and complex cells of the primary visual cortex (V1).","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"As visual information goes from the simple cells to the complex cells and then to other brain areas, the receptive fields become larger and more specialized.","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"That is especially true for the inferior temporal cortex.","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-3-h03","text":"The Inferior Temporal Cortex"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A cell that learns to respond to the sight of an object initially responds mainly when it perceives it from the same angle, but after enough experience it responds from other viewpoints and distances .","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The inferior temporal cortex exchanges information with the prefrontal cortex with connections that are especially important for identifying difficult or ambiguous patterns .","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One way to describe it is that the prefrontal cortex forms hypotheses about the object and feeds them back to the temporal cortex for confirmation or disconfirmation.","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The inferior temporal cortex responds to more than just the patterns of light and dark that stimulate area V1.","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"As we might expect, damage to the ventral pathway of the cortex leads to specialized deficits.","sourcePrintedPage":177,"sourcePdfPage":195,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Within the inferior temporal cortex, several areas detect particular shapes, and brain damage can yield remarkable results.","sourcePrintedPage":178,"sourcePdfPage":196,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One man with brain damage could recognize almost anything he saw except the numbers 2 through 9, which always appeared to him as a tangle of black lines .","sourcePrintedPage":178,"sourcePdfPage":196,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Part of the parahippocampal cortex (next to the hippocampus) responds mostly to the sight of places.","sourcePrintedPage":178,"sourcePdfPage":196,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The brain is remarkably adept at detecting the kinds of motion produced by people and animals.","sourcePrintedPage":178,"sourcePdfPage":196,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-3-h04","text":"Recognizing Faces"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Civilization depends on knowing whether to trust or distrust someone, even someone you haven’t seen in months or years.","sourcePrintedPage":178,"sourcePdfPage":196,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When confronted with two right-side-up faces (right pair), they expressed no significant preference between a realistic one and a distorted one .","sourcePrintedPage":178,"sourcePdfPage":196,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Cortical cells that respond strongly to faces also respond somewhat to face-like objects .","sourcePrintedPage":178,"sourcePdfPage":196,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Depending on the intensity and duration of stimulation, the result was either a difficulty in perceiving faces or a vivid distortion of faces.","sourcePrintedPage":178,"sourcePdfPage":196,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Monkeys also have trouble recognizing faces during electrical stimulation of an area corresponding to the fusiform gyrus .","sourcePrintedPage":178,"sourcePdfPage":196,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People vary considerably in their ability to recognize faces, and not because of a lack of interest.","sourcePrintedPage":179,"sourcePdfPage":197,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with the worst recognition are said to have prosopagnosia (PROSSoh-pag-NOH-see-ah), meaning impaired ability to recognize faces.","sourcePrintedPage":179,"sourcePdfPage":197,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In his words, “I have had difficulty recognizing faces for as long as I can remember.","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"My problem with recognizing faces extends not only to my nearest and dearest but also to myself.","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"He remarked that he seldom enjoyed watching movies or television programs because he had trouble keeping track of the characters.","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The other hypothesis is that we evolved mechanisms for recognizing complex patterns, of which faces happen to be the best and most common example .","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Additional evidence for a predisposition is that people who were blind from birth exhibit elevated activity in the fusiform gyrus when they feel models of faces .","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-3-h05","text":"Motion Perception"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It might be a possible mate, something you could hunt and eat, or something that wants to eat you.","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"You need to identify where it is going, and how fast.","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The brain is set up to make those calculations quickly.","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-3-h06","text":"The Middle Temporal Cortex"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Two areas especially important for motion perception are area MT (for middle temporal cortex), also known as area V5 (Figure 5.27), and an adjacent region, area MST (medial superior temporal cortex).","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"These areas receive input mostly from the magnocellular path , which detects overall patterns and movement.","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most cells in area MT respond selectively when something moves at a particular speed in a particular direction .","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"MT cells detect acceleration or deceleration as well as absolute speed , and they respond to motion in all three dimensions .","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Area MT also responds to photographs that imply movement, such as a photo of people running .","sourcePrintedPage":180,"sourcePdfPage":198,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Neurons in areas MT and the ventral part of MST respond briskly if something moves relative to the background, but they exhibit little response if the object and the background both move in the same direction and speed .","sourcePrintedPage":181,"sourcePdfPage":199,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-3-h07","text":"Motion Blindness"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The result is motion blindness , being able to see objects but unable to see whether they are moving or, if so, which direction and how fast .","sourcePrintedPage":181,"sourcePdfPage":199,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with motion blindness are better at reaching for a moving object than at describing its motion , but in all aspects of dealing with visual motion, they are far behind other people.","sourcePrintedPage":181,"sourcePdfPage":199,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Motion blindness in the absence of other dysfunction is a rare condition.","sourcePrintedPage":181,"sourcePdfPage":199,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Someone who was walking would appear to her as “restless,” but she would not know which direction the person was going.","sourcePrintedPage":181,"sourcePdfPage":199,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"She could not cross a street without help, because she could not tell which cars were moving, or how fast.","sourcePrintedPage":181,"sourcePdfPage":199,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because this experience seems so odd, neurologists for many years resisted the idea of motion blindness.","sourcePrintedPage":181,"sourcePdfPage":199,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Several patients were reported who apparently became motion blind after brain damage, but most scientists ignored or disbelieved the reports.","sourcePrintedPage":181,"sourcePdfPage":199,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After the discovery of area MT from monkey research, researchers saw a mechanism whereby motion blindness could occur, and they came to accept the reports of motion blindness.","sourcePrintedPage":181,"sourcePdfPage":199,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The opposite of motion blindness also occurs: Some people are blind except for the ability to detect movement.","sourcePrintedPage":182,"sourcePdfPage":200,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m5-3-h08","text":"In Closing: .","printedPage":180,"pdfPage":198,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":45},{"text":"Additional evidence for a predisposition is that people who were .","printedPage":180,"pdfPage":198,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":46},{"text":"Human newborns come into the world predisposed to pay more attention of the occipital cortex known as the occipital face area.","printedPage":178,"pdfPage":196,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":86},{"text":"At the as area V5 (Figure 5.27), and an adjacent region, area MST (medial superior temporal cortex).","printedPage":180,"pdfPage":198,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":52},{"text":"These areas receive input mostly from the magnocellular path , which detects overall patterns and movement.","printedPage":180,"pdfPage":198,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":53},{"text":"Most cells in area MT respond selectively when something moves at a particular speed in a particular direction .","printedPage":180,"pdfPage":198,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":54},{"text":"MT cells detect acceleration or deceleration as well as absolute speed , and they respond to motion in all three dimensions .","printedPage":180,"pdfPage":198,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":55},{"text":"Area MT also responds to photographs that imply movement, such as a photo of people running .","printedPage":180,"pdfPage":198,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":56},{"text":"Neurons in areas MT and the ventral part of MST respond briskly if something moves relative to the background, but they exhibit little response if the object and the background both move in the same direction and speed .","printedPage":181,"pdfPage":199,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":57},{"text":"Given that the magnocellular path is color insensitive, MT is also color insensitive.","printedPage":180,"pdfPage":198,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":92},{"text":"That kind of experience occurs when you move forward or backward or tilt your head.","printedPage":180,"pdfPage":198,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":93},{"text":"When you move your head or eyes from left to right, everything in your visual field moves across your retina as if the world itself had moved right to left.","printedPage":181,"pdfPage":199,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":94},{"text":"(Go ahead and try it.) Yet the world seems stationary, because nothing moved relative to anything people.","printedPage":181,"pdfPage":199,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":60},{"text":"Motion blindness in the absence of other dysfunction is a rare condition.","printedPage":181,"pdfPage":199,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":61},{"text":"Someone who was walking would appear to her as “restless,” but she would not know which direction the person was going.","printedPage":181,"pdfPage":199,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":62},{"text":"She could them.","printedPage":181,"pdfPage":199,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":96},{"text":"People with full color vision can imagine what it would be like to be color deficient, but it is difficult to imagine having motion blindness.","printedPage":181,"pdfPage":199,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":97},{"text":"You wonder what it would be like to be motion blind.","printedPage":181,"pdfPage":199,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":98},{"text":"In short, during a voluntary eye movement, you become motion blind for a split second.","printedPage":182,"pdfPage":200,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":99},{"text":"Perhaps now you understand a little better what people with motion blindness experience all the Pitch perception, auditory cortex activity, and sound localization explain different parts of hearing."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The book also considers differences in hearing and the effects of deafness, attention, and aging. Distinguish the physical characteristics of sound from the perceptual interpretations the nervous system makes."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-1-study-1","text":"What sound is"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sound begins with pressure changes transmitted through a medium such as air. Frequency is closely related to perceived pitch, whereas intensity contributes to perceived loudness; perception is also influenced by context and the listener's auditory system. The ear converts mechanical vibration into neural signaling. The outer ear collects sound, the middle ear transmits vibration through tiny bones, and the inner ear contains fluid-filled structures that respond to it. Do not confuse the physical properties of a sound wave with how a person experiences that sound."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-1-study-2","text":"The cochlea and pitch"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Within the cochlea, movement of its structures bends hair-cell receptors and leads to changes in auditory-nerve signaling. Different positions along the basilar membrane respond best to different frequencies, providing a place-based basis for pitch. Timing patterns in neural firing also help encode pitch, particularly for lower frequencies. Because auditory experience arises from several forms of coding, neither a simple 'one frequency–one neuron' view nor a solely temporal account fully captures all pitch perception."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-1-study-3","text":"From auditory pathways to localization"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Signals travel from auditory nerves through several brainstem and thalamic stations before reaching auditory cortex. The nervous system uses differences in sound arrival time and intensity at the two ears, together with other cues, to estimate where a sound originates. Localization becomes more difficult when a cue is missing or misleading. Auditory cortex contributes to analysis of complex sound patterns, yet hearing depends on processing distributed across multiple structures."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m6-1-study-4","text":"Differences among listeners"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hearing varies with age, experience, and sensory damage. Deafness is not a single condition and can involve conductive problems, cochlear damage, or central neural pathways. Attention can also influence what a person notices amid competing sounds; an intact ear does not guarantee that every signal becomes conscious. When revising, follow the sound from pressure wave to mechanical vibration, receptor response, auditory pathway, and meaningful perception."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-1-h01","text":"Sound and the Ear"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We attend to hearing to extract useful information.","sourcePrintedPage":188,"sourcePdfPage":206,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If you hear footsteps in your home or a snapped twig in the forest, you know you are not alone.","sourcePrintedPage":188,"sourcePdfPage":206,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If you hear breathing, you know a person or animal is close.","sourcePrintedPage":188,"sourcePdfPage":206,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If you recognize the sound of a familiar voice, you know that all is well.","sourcePrintedPage":188,"sourcePdfPage":206,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Under optimum conditions, human hearing is sensitive to sounds that vibrate the eardrum by less than one-tenth the diameter of an atom, and some people can detect a difference between sounds as little as 1/30 the interval between two piano notes .","sourcePrintedPage":188,"sourcePdfPage":206,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-1-h02","text":"Physics and Psychology of Sound"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sound waves are periodic compressions of air, water, or other media, varying in amplitude and frequency.","sourcePrintedPage":188,"sourcePdfPage":206,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In general, sounds of greater amplitude seem louder, but a rapidly talking person seems louder than slow music of the same amplitude.","sourcePrintedPage":188,"sourcePdfPage":206,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The frequency of a sound is the number of compressions per second, measured in hertz (Hz, cycles per second).","sourcePrintedPage":188,"sourcePdfPage":206,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The height of each wave represents the amplitude, and the number of waves per second represents the frequency.","sourcePrintedPage":188,"sourcePdfPage":206,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"frequencies, because the ability to perceive high frequencies decreases with age and exposure to loud noises.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In addition to amplitude and pitch, the third aspect of sound is timbre (TAM-ber), meaning tone quality or tone complexity.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Different musical instruments playing the same note sound different, as do people singing the same note.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An instrument playing a note at any frequency also produces notes at multiples of that frequency, the harmonics of the principal note.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-1-h03","text":"Structures of the Ear"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The outer ear includes the pinna , the familiar structure of flesh and cartilage attached to each side of the head.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"By altering the reflections of sound waves, the pinna helps us locate the source of a sound.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We have to learn to use that information because all pinnas are shaped differently .","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Sound waves passing through the auditory canal (Figure 6.2) enter the middle ear, a structure that had to evolve when ancient fish evolved into land animals.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because animal tissues respond to water vibrations almost the same way that water itself does, fish have relatively simple hearing receptors that would not respond well to vibrations in the air .","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The structures of the middle ear and inner ear evolved to amplify sound vibrations.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When sound waves reach the middle ear, they vibrate the tympanic membrane , or eardrum.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When the stirrup vibrates the oval window, it sets into motion the fluid in the cochlea (KOCK-lee-uh), the snailshaped structure of the inner ear.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-1-h04","text":"Pitch Perception"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"According to the frequency theory in its original form, the basilar membrane vibrates in synchrony with sound waves, causing auditory nerve axons to produce action potentials at the same frequency.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, a sound at 50 Hz would cause 50 action potentials per second in the auditory nerve.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The downfall of this theory in its simplest form is that the refractory period limits the maximum firing rate of any neuron to about 1000 Hz, far short of the highest frequencies we hear.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although any single receptor is limited in its firing frequency, a group of receptors can have a pattern like the one represented below.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Each sound wave produces responses in the receptors that are phase-locked to the sound wave but not to one another.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A soft tone stimulates fewer neurons for each peak of the sound wave, and louder tones stimulate progressively more of them.","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"the basilar membrane are bound together too tightly for any part to resonate like a piano string.","sourcePrintedPage":190,"sourcePdfPage":208,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-1-h05","text":"The Auditory Cortex"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"As information from the auditory system passes through subcortical areas, axons cross over in the midbrain to enable each hemisphere of the forebrain to get most of its input, but not all of it, from the opposite ear.","sourcePrintedPage":191,"sourcePdfPage":209,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The visual and auditory systems differ in this respect: Whereas damage to the primary visual cortex (area V1) leaves someone blind, damage to the primary auditory cortex does not produce deafness.","sourcePrintedPage":192,"sourcePdfPage":210,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with damage to the primary auditory cortex have trouble with speech and music, but they identify and localize single sounds reasonably well .","sourcePrintedPage":192,"sourcePdfPage":210,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cortex is not necessary for all hearing, but for processing what the information means.","sourcePrintedPage":192,"sourcePdfPage":210,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When researchers record from cells in the primary auditory cortex while playing pure tones, they find that most cells have a preferred tone.","sourcePrintedPage":192,"sourcePdfPage":210,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although some cells in the auditory cortex respond well to a single tone, most cells respond best to a complex sound, such as a dominant tone and its harmonics .","sourcePrintedPage":192,"sourcePdfPage":210,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Surrounding the primary auditory cortex are the secondary auditory cortex and other areas that respond mainly to meaningful","sourcePrintedPage":192,"sourcePdfPage":210,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The auditory cortex is important not just for hearing but also for thinking about anything related to hearing.","sourcePrintedPage":192,"sourcePdfPage":210,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-1-h06","text":"Sound Localization"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Human sound localization is less accurate than visual localization but nevertheless impressive.","sourcePrintedPage":193,"sourcePdfPage":211,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most birds’ alarm calls increase gradually in loudness, making them difficult for a predator to localize.","sourcePrintedPage":193,"sourcePdfPage":211,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For high-frequency sounds, with a wavelength shorter than the width of the head, the head creates a sound shadow (Figure 6.7), making the sound louder for the closer ear.","sourcePrintedPage":193,"sourcePdfPage":211,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In adult humans, this mechanism produces accurate sound localization for frequencies above 2,000 to 3,000 Hz and less accurate localizations for lower frequencies.","sourcePrintedPage":193,"sourcePdfPage":211,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"How much out of phase depends on the frequency of the sound, the size of the head, and the direction of the sound.","sourcePrintedPage":194,"sourcePdfPage":212,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The reason is that sounds travel faster in water than in air, so a sound","sourcePrintedPage":194,"sourcePdfPage":212,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most can localize a sudden sound of any frequency by the times of onset.","sourcePrintedPage":194,"sourcePdfPage":212,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"All of these methods require learning, because as a human head grows, the distance between ears increases, and humans need to recalibrate how they localize sounds .","sourcePrintedPage":194,"sourcePdfPage":212,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Humans can also localize whether a sound is coming from above or below, although less accurately than left vs. right.","sourcePrintedPage":194,"sourcePdfPage":212,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The pinnae have an irregular shape that filters sound frequencies differently depending on their location up or down, front or back.","sourcePrintedPage":194,"sourcePdfPage":212,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-1-h07","text":"Individual Differences"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An estimated 4 percent of people have amusia , commonly called “tone deafness” .","sourcePrintedPage":194,"sourcePdfPage":212,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although they are not really unable to hear differences in tones, they do not detect a change less than about the difference between C and C-sharp .","sourcePrintedPage":194,"sourcePdfPage":212,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They usually cannot tell whether someone is singing off-key, and they do not detect a “wrong” note in a melody.","sourcePrintedPage":194,"sourcePdfPage":212,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Absolute pitch (or “perfect pitch”) is the ability to hear a note and identify it—for example, “That’s a B flat.” Genetic predisposition contributes , but early musical training is also important.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In those languages, the meaning of a sound depends on its pitch, and people learn to pay close attention to pitch.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In the traditional manner of testing for absolute pitch, a researcher plays a pure note and asks someone to name it.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"By that method, only about one person in ten thousand qualifies, and we are tempted to think of absolute pitch as a superpower.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-1-h08","text":"Deafness"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although few people are totally unable to hear, many people have enough impairment to prevent speech comprehension.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because people with conductive deafness have a normal cochlea and auditory nerve, they readily hear their own voices, conducted through the bones of the skull directly to the cochlea, bypassing the middle ear.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because they hear themselves clearly, they may accuse others of talking too softly.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Nerve deafness , or inner-ear deafness , results from damage to the cochlea, the hair cells, or the auditory nerve.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Nerve deafness can be inherited, it can result from disease, or it can result from exposure to loud noises.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is common in people who have lost their hearing but rare in people with lifelong deafness.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It has many causes , but in some cases it resembles phantom limb.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Occasionally, people with hearing loss experience auditory hallucinations, probably because something is stimulating the otherwise inactive synapses .","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-1-h09","text":"Hearing, Attention, and Old Age"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They especially have trouble understanding speech in a noisy room or when someone speaks rapidly.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Part of the explanation is that the brain areas responsible for language comprehension have become less active .","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This trend might be just a natural deterioration, or it might be a reaction to prolonged degradation of auditory input.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If someone delays getting hearing aids, the language cortex doesn’t get its typical input, and it becomes less responsive.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"As cochlear hair cells die because of the aging process or anything else, the auditory cortex receives less input than usual.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"That process improves hearing most of the time, but in a noisy environment, it increases the background noise just as much as the conversation.","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m6-1-h10","text":"In Closing: Functions of example, the way you say “that was interesting” could indicate approval (it really was interesting), sarcasm (it really was boring), or suspicion (you think someone was hinting something).","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207},{"type":"bullet","text":"The functioning of the ear is complex enough to resemble a Rube Goldberg Anatomists distinguish the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207},{"type":"bullet","text":"These bones, the smallest bones in the body, are sometimes known by their English names (hammer, anvil, and stirrup) and sometimes by their Latin names (malleus, incus, and stapes).","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207},{"type":"bullet","text":"As in a hydraulic pump, the vibrations of the tympanic membrane amplify into more forceful vibrations of the smaller stirrup, converting sound waves into waves of greater pressure on the oval window.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207},{"type":"bullet","text":"To understand speech or enjoy music you have to detect the frequencies of sounds.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207},{"type":"bullet","text":"In this way the auditory nerve can produce volleys of impulses for sounds up to about 4,000 per second, even though no individual axon approaches that frequency.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":189,"sourcePdfPage":207},{"type":"bullet","text":"The second mechanism of pitch perception is the place theory.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":190,"sourcePdfPage":208},{"type":"bullet","text":"Originally, this theory suggested that the basilar membrane resembles the strings of a piano.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":190,"sourcePdfPage":208},{"type":"bullet","text":"A high-pitched sound sets up a traveling wave that peaks sharply at some point along the basilar membrane.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":191,"sourcePdfPage":209},{"type":"bullet","text":"Low frequency sounds vibrate hair cells near the apex, and high frequency sounds vibrate hair cells farther toward the base.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":191,"sourcePdfPage":209},{"type":"bullet","text":"The information ultimately reaches the primary auditory cortex (area A1) in the superior temporal cortex, as illustrated in Figure 6.5.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":191,"sourcePdfPage":209},{"type":"bullet","text":"An area in the temporal cortex called the planum temporale processes the experience you have of a sound source moving from one place to another.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":191,"sourcePdfPage":209},{"type":"bullet","text":"The auditory cortex provides what researchers call a tonotopic map of sounds, as depicted in and not others.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213},{"type":"bullet","text":"Damage to part of the cochlea is like an amputation: If the auditory cortex no longer in a particular range report ringing in the ears in the same range, suggesting that something else is activating the vacated aids.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213},{"type":"bullet","text":"The rest of the explanation relates to filtering out irrelevant sounds.","headingId":"bp14-m6-1-h09","sourcePrintedPage":195,"sourcePdfPage":213},{"type":"bullet","text":"It adjusts by facilitating the excitatory synapses and decreasing the inhibitory synapses, “turning up the volume knob” to increase the .","printedPage":195,"pdfPage":213,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":78},{"text":"The two categories of hearing loss are conductive deafness and nerve
